## The idea

`mazegenerator` uses randomized depth-first search with backtracking, often
called the *recursive backtracker*. Despite the name, this implementation is
iterative: a list is used as a stack, so it does not depend on R's recursion
limit.

Start by creating a small reproducible maze:

```{r create}
library(mazegenerator)

maze <- generate_maze(8, 12, start = c(1, 1), seed = 42)
maze
```

At each step, the generator:

1. finds the orthogonal neighbors of the current cell;
2. randomly chooses one that has not been visited;
3. carves a passage and pushes that cell onto the stack;
4. returns to the previous cell when it reaches a dead end.

The process ends after every cell has been visited.

```{r plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
plot_maze(maze)
```

## Why the result is a perfect maze

Every new passage connects the visited region to exactly one previously
unvisited cell. Therefore the passages never create a cycle. Because generation
continues until every cell is visited, the result is also connected. A connected
graph without cycles is a tree, so there is exactly one simple route between
any pair of cells.

For a maze with *rows × columns* cells, the generator creates exactly one fewer
unique passage than the number of cells.

```{r properties}
length(maze$passages)
maze$rows * maze$cols - 1
```

## Finding a route

`solve_maze()` applies A-star search to the passage graph. Manhattan distance
is an admissible heuristic because maze movement is orthogonal and each step
has the same cost.

```{r solve, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
solution <- solve_maze(maze)
head(solution)
plot_maze(maze, solution = solution)
```

The same function accepts a matrix in which selected values represent walkable
cells. When diagonal movement is enabled, Euclidean distance and diagonal step
costs are used so the search still returns a shortest path.
